messages.subject: Variogram interpretation - Model fit
messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris,

I'm hoping to estimate AKDEs for an overlap analysis and I'm writing to consult about model fit. All my study animals seem to show range residency according to variogram shape and to model selection (best models are either OUF or OU). Yet, visual inspection shows that many of the models selected do not fit the variogram well; I have attached some examples. These animals are non-migratory adults, I'm using GPS data, and transmitters only worked during the daytime. My question, then, is if I should be concerned about the fit of these models, and how to proceed if I should improve them. I'm interested in one estimate per animal and we have 35 tracked individuals.

Thanks in advance for your help,

Paula

messages.subject: Re: Variogram interpretation - Model fit
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paula,

You definitely have something happening on a daily cycle and on an annual cycle. The daily cycle could either be movement, where they go to particular spots at certain times, or where the signal drops out periodically because they go into a burrow or something. The annual cycle is probably a small "migration" during the cold part of the year, or something like that. There are models where you can test for that in vignette('periodogram'), but I haven't coded the home range estimation to properly condition on those models yet, as that is a little complicated.

With using the basic models in the package like you are, you might try segmenting the data into summer/winter and performing separate range estimates on the two distributions per individual. The daily periodicities aren't as hampering to the home-range estimation as the migration is.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: 3D Home Range
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adrian,

As we have yet to publish a paper on the methods, these aren't well maintained features of the package, but if you run into any issues then feel free to submit a support request and I will fix it.

The extra ingredient you need over a 2D AKDE is a fitted movement model for vertical axis. You can do this by running most methods like variogram() and ctmm.select() with axes="z" instead of the default axes=c("x","y").

After you have the 2D movement model and the vertical movement model, you supply both to the akde() function in the CTMM and VMM arguments.

Plotting methods are not yet coded up for 3D UDs.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: thinning data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,
We have automated telemetry data for birds, sampled continuously (day and night) at fairly high temporal resolution (every 2-5 mins)...with occasional gaps in detection when birds are in dense vegetation, or briefly outside the telemetry array. Between ~20 and 60% of our detections occur at night for these birds, depending on individual. Previous studies estimating home ranges for diurnal birds do not typically have information on nocturnal locations. We are thinking of either removing nocturnal location estimates, or thinning them to one random detection per hour. We are concerned that the high temporal resolution of nocturnal detections while individuals are largely stationary will "drown out" the signal of space use during the day. A quick analysis looking at HR estimates for a few birds with and without the nocturnal detections reveals that when we include nocturnal detections 1) the HR area estimates are lower, 2) the tau position estimates are larger, and 3) the shape of the HR changes. A review of the literature confirms that many data sets from GPS/Argos trackers simply do not collect data while individuals are inactive, so there is some precedent for leaving out the nocturnal detections. I wonder however, whether we might be potentially introducing some bias by removing or thinning nocturnal detections? What are your thoughts or recommendations on this matter?

In case this influences the matter, we are incorporating estimates of error in the modeling process, based on calibration data from transmitters at known locations.

Thank you!
Jenny

messages.subject: Re: thinning data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jenny,

If you have two behavioral states on a diurnal species like this, then its probably not good to fit one stationary movement model to both behavior states. The first thing you would want to do is segment the data and fit separate movement models. Further complications might warrant even more data wrangling: like is the nocturnal behavior centered on one nest or does it vary, etc..

With two behavioral states, there are really two distinct distributions with two different meanings, and where the nocturnal distribution is much smaller than the day distribution. I would estimate these distributions separately with their separate movement models (and separate/segmented data). The more important range is probably the larger diurnal range, but you might also want to report the daily/aggregate range by averaging the two with mean() and appropriate weights argument (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/mean.html).

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Warning messages
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I ran ctmm for akde estimation and I am getting three warning messages at the end of the process. I wonder if you can help me to figured out what I should do to get rid of this warning in the future.

This is the chunk of code that I used and the warnings at the end. Thanks in advance.
All the best,

tracks <- as.telemetry(mydata.csv")
trackIDs <- names(tracks)
folder <- paste(getwd(),"/shp/ctmm_central", sep="")

for(i in 1:length(trackIDs)) {
  track_i <- tracks[i]
  names(track_i) <- "1"
  track_h <- track_i$'1'
  GUESS <- ctmm.guess(track_h,interactive=FALSE)
  print(i)
  FIT <- ctmm.fit(track_h,GUESS)
  UD <- akde(track_h,FIT)
  assign(paste("UD", trackIDs[i], sep = ""), UD)
  writeShapefile(UD,folder,file=trackIDs[i],level.UD=c(0.5,0.95),level=0.95)
}

Warning messages:
1: In cov.loglike(hess, grad) :
  MLE is near a boundary or optimizer failed.
2: In ctmm.fit(track_h, GUESS) :
  pREML failure: indefinite ML Hessian or divergent REML gradient.
3: In cov.loglike(DIFF$hessian, grad) :
  MLE is near a boundary or optimizer failed.

messages.subject: path reconstruction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I have automated telemetry data collected on a few hundred birds, with a typical (but gappy) sampling rate of 2 to 4 minutes. I used tags at known locations to develop models that predict error for each detection based on covariates. I have a few things that I want to do with these data in ctmm, and would like to make sure I am using the package correctly.

1) Incorporating error: Since we already had an error estimate for each point (in meters), I named this column “VAR.xy” in my data, made sure this column was included in my telemetry object, and incorporated into models like so, where my_stack is my data formatted as a move stack:

yourAnimals <- as.telemetry(my_stack, keep = c('VAR.xy'))

GUESS <- ctmm.guess(yourAnimals[[1]], CTMM = ctmm(error=TRUE), interactive=FALSE)

FIT <- ctmm.select(yourAnimals[[1]], GUESS,  trace = T,  verbose = T)

I would like to confirm that I am doing this correctly in ctmm, since my data do not have the same structure as the Argos data in the examples.

2) Probabilistic path reconstruction: Some of the birds’ tracks have greater error (up to ~ 350 m), and are sparser with some gaps varying from a few hours to a few days. We want to use these data to explore exposure to avian malaria, so it would be very helpful to predict over some of the short time gaps, or at least improve our existing location estimates for these birds. The location estimates are based on triangulation, and are thus “blind” to estimates at nearby times.

2.1)   Do I understand correctly that with Kriging we may be able to predict location at the observed times with a bit more precision, as we can leverage the auto-correlation structure of the data? If so, how can we estimate this precision? An error ellipse for each location estimate would be ideal.

2.2) To explore how far we can reasonably interpolate into time gaps I have thinned the points on a fairly high-resolution individual (median lag of 4 mins) to make artificial gaps of varying duration. To assess the spatial accuracy of predicted location I compared predicted (and simulated) locations to the “true” locations that were thinned. Is this approach a defensible way of figuring out how far out into a gap it might be reasonable to predict (or simulate)? I assume the determination for this bird is not necessarily relevant for the ~ 250 others? Is there a better way to determine a reasonable dt.max argument, perhaps based on the tau estimate?

2.3) The predict function (based on the best OU error model) is giving point estimates far closer to the actual thinned locations than the simulate function. For instance, with my fake 12 minute gaps I am getting point estimates 143 (±114m) from the “true” path, and the simulate function is giving me point estimates 228 (±161m) from the “true” path. Considering the mean error for this individual is ~ 140m neither of these seems too terrible, and I figured interpolating with dt.max of 12 mins is OK. Since the predict function is returning better point estimates I am inclined to use this. However, it would be nice to also have some measure of confidence at both the observed and interpolated points, and I am not sure I can get this with predict…perhaps I need to use a lot of simulated tracks?

3) I noticed that the FAQ mentions not to save the workspace. This feels like a dumb R question, but....what then is the recommended method to save model results? I have automated R to output the model summary, and the AKDE raster and shapefiles for each individual, but then found myself wanting to go back and do something else with the model output later and had to re-run. I am probably missing something obvious.

Thank you for any insight. It is exciting to learn how to use this package!

Best,

Jenny

messages.subject: Re: path reconstruction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jenny,

1.) Looks good.

2.1) After what you've done (error calibration & movement model selection) you run the selected movement model and calibrated tracking data through predict(). The output will have both location point estimates and error ellipses in the columns of the dataframe.

2.2) That sounds reasonable to me. For coverage you might try looking at the standardized prediction errors. I.e., if

d <- predicted_location - triangulated_location
S <- predicted_COV + triangulated_COV

then (d %*% solve(S) %*% d) should be (approximately) chi^2 with two degrees of freedom. But as far as how fast the error ellipse will expand out, that will be dictated by the tau values.

2.3) simulate does not give estimates, but randomly sampled trajectories that are consistent with the model and data. predict's point estimate should be closer to the truth than most realizations from simulate. predict output should have variance/covariance columns corresponding to the point estimates (COV.xx, COV.yy, COV.xy, or VAR.xy). You don't choose between simulate and predict based on accuracy, but based on use case.

3) I recommend saving objects that take a long time to compute to an R data file via save().

Best,
Chris
